subtopic: MR. FORTIN-LATE DELIVERY OF FRENCH HANSARD
MR. FORTIN-LATE DELIVERY OF FRENCH HANSARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.
I have noticed every morning, to my great annoyance and to that of each of my colleagues, that the French version of Hansard gets to us some hours after the English one. I should be grateful, Mr. Speaker, if this situation were put right immediately. This quite unacceptable delay holds up the work of members who speak only French.
I consider that bilingualism must be applied as efficiently as possible in the House if we are to set the example for all levels of the federal civil service. I believe that monolingual francophones have a right to get just as swift service in their own language as monolingual anglophones do, and that no technical obstacle should prevent the application of this principle.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise), I move:
That the Speaker of the House of Commons be authorized to take whatever technical measures are necessary for the French version of Hansard to be published as soon as possible every day, like the English version, so that both versions may be available to all members early in the morning.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. FORTIN-LATE DELIVERY OF FRENCH HANSARD
speechtext:
I would point out to the hon. member that his proposal is a formal motion and not a question of privilege. He may wish to move it on motions under Standing Order 43.
In any case, I acknowledge that the hon. member has raised a serious point which deserves the attention of the Chair; I will give close and conscientious study to the hon. member's suggestion that the French version of Hansard appear at the same time as the English version.
The hon. member will admit, however, that there is a certain problem and I suspect that the reason for the delayed publication of the French edition is that especially on some days, most speeches are delivered in English. Now those speeches must be translated before appearing in Hansard, which necessarily involves a delay.
It is possible, however, that there would be a technical way to cope with that difficulty and I will convey the hon. member's complaint to the attention of those who are responsible for the preparation and daily publication of Hansard in French as well as in English.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PAYMENTS ON WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY FOR 1973-74 CROP YEAR

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PAYMENTS ON WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY FOR 1973-74 CROP YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as has been the custom for the past two years, I should like to again this year inform the House, and then send information to all producers in the prairie region, about the initial payments for wheat, oats and barley for the 1973-74 crop year. The practice is to give this information to farmers now, prior to seeding, so that it can play a part in their plans for the next crop year beginning on August 1, 1973.
The initial payment for No. 1. western red spring wheat will be fixed at $1.76 a bushel, which is the same as in the current crop year. The initial payment for No. 3. western six-row barley will be $1.20 a bushel, an increase of 15 cents over the level presently in effect. This is in line with some of the requests from farm organizations. The initial payment for No. 2. western oats will be 80 cents a bushel which is an increase of 10 cents over the current crop year level. All initial payments are "basis in store Thunder Bay and Vancouver". The initial payments for the grades of wheat, barley and oats other than the basic grades I have mentioned will be established by the Canadian Wheat Board and announced at a later date.
It is our expectation that the higher level of initial payments for barley and oats, in addition to the higher level of assured deliveries which will be referred to in letters going to the producers, will encourage producers to increase feed grain acreage over the acreage sown in 1972 and that they will do this even though an increase is expected in the acreage that will be sown.
Producers are also being encouraged to increase production of rapeseed this year in view of the excellent market prospects for the sale of all of these grains and because of the importance of holding our customers in this area as well in making the best use of the acreage available in the Canadian production area now and in the future.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PAYMENTS ON WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY FOR 1973-74 CROP YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in replying briefly to the minister responsible for the Wheat Board I would hope that on other occasions he would give longer notice to opposition members who are expected to comment on * such statements. This is only courtesy, and I would strongly urge the minister to take this course in the future. In this instance, the statement was received about two minutes before he stood up to make it.

February 22, 1973
Initial Payments, Wheat, Oats and Barley
As far as the prices are concerned, I think the initial payment for barley of $1.20 is in line with what we on this side of the House have been urging. I am disappointed, though, that there is no guarantee to purchase a set amount of barley and I think this is really the critical item of the three items the minister mentioned. I am also disappointed that he did not say anything about a cash advance in his statement. It seems that if farmers are to receive these amounts of money it will be very necessary for them this spring to have some funds by way of cash advances to help them put their crops in.
A guarantee, though, is possibly more important because I believe, after talking to a good many farmers in western Canada, that as markets are at the present time, unless the government can guarantee to take all or virtually all of the feed grain produced in western Canada we still face the possibility that there will be a very heavy emphasis on wheat production. I think this is very critical. I hope the minister will realize the importance of our feed grain markets being maintained this year in particular, since I think this will be a crisis year for the production of feed grains in Canada. We will hopefully see an enlarged market domestically, and over the next year or two the demand for feed grain will be even heavier.
I believe that the prices announced by the government are realistic. However, for this year at least I think the government should guarantee to take a set number of bushels rather than simply proceed on the assumption that in view of the price of the grain farmers will automatically grow the required amount.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PAYMENTS ON WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY FOR 1973-74 CROP YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the initial price guaranteed by the government is not unexpected. If we are to have the amount of feed grain or barley we are going to need this year, this is the minimum that could be set as the initial price. It could be argued that the initial payment should be higher, because in the case of feed barley, which is the grade that moves best and is produced in greatest amount, the initial price will be less than the price announced. I hope the minister will announce the initial prices for other grades of barley very soon.
The critical area in crop production in western Canada is probably rapeseed. I notice that the minister says that producers are also encouraged to increase the production of rapeseed this year. That is a nice phrase, but in point of fact the government has done nothing to encourage producers to grow rapeseed this year in sufficient acreages and quantities to serve the markets that have been developing.
Surely the minister is aware that the pricing situation in regard to rapeseed is chaotic. Surely he is aware that one price is being paid at one point in Saskatchewan while a few miles away another price is being paid. Surely he is aware that delivery opportunities between the producers of Saskatchewan and those of other provinces are unequal, and that transportation of rapeseed by rail has not been satisfactory.
It is not good enough for the minister simply to insert that sentence in his statement and leave it at that. If we are to produce the amount we need I suggest the minister must come back to the House soon and announce the
policy of the government so that the farmers will plant the rapeseed acreages that we are going to need this year. In view of the guaranteed initial prices for wheat and barley and given orderly delivery for those grains and a clear road ahead for the farmer, and in view of the marketing of rapeseed in the past, one does not need to do a lot of guessing to know what could possibly occur.
Finally, the minister should clarify his position regarding the so-called two-price system for wheat. Instead of sending out questionnaires and trying to conduct a plebiscite by mail, which incidentally leaves out significant numbers of people with a stake in such payments, the minister had better come to the House and tell the House what his policy is, so we can then refer the matter to the standing committee where it can be properly discussed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the House is aware, on learning yesterday of this tragic event I, on behalf of the government and people of Canada, sent a message of condolence through our ambassador in Cairo to the foreign ministers of Libya and Egypt.

What is all too clear, however, is that, as a result of a conscious act, up to 100 innocent persons aboard a regularly scheduled flight of a civilian airliner are dead. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. In view of the fact the rates for advance booking charters have finally been set at the level of about $187, and in view of the fact these rates are some $80 more than the rates for a comparable trip originating in Britain, will the minister inform the House whether he has any intention of asking the Canadian Transport Commission to revise its rate-setting procedures so that Canadian travellers can benefit from the advantages of fair competition in this field?

subsubtopic: ADVANCE BOOKING CHARTER REGULATIONS-REQUEST THAT CANADIAN TRANSPORT COMMISSION REVIEW RATE-SETTING PROCEDURE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the competition that the Canadian Transport Commission governs is that which involves planes chartered for flights outside the country. However, we do not consider a plane chartered in England to bring passengers to Canada and take them back to England as a competitor, because the clientele involved is not the same. And so it can happen that English companies perform the service at rates that are patently lower than ours.

subsubtopic: ADVANCE BOOKING CHARTER REGULATIONS-REQUEST THAT CANADIAN TRANSPORT COMMISSION REVIEW RATE-SETTING PROCEDURE
speechtext: Considering that it would be very difficult for most Canadians to understand why it should cost almost twice as much for Canadians to travel from Toronto to London and return than for British residents to travel from London to Toronto and return, can the minister assure the House that he will ask the CTC to study the whole pricing procedure, particularly with a view to ensuring that there is competition in the pricing structure in Canada?

subsubtopic: ADVANCE BOOKING CHARTER REGULATIONS-REQUEST THAT CANADIAN TRANSPORT COMMISSION REVIEW RATE-SETTING PROCEDURE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Transport Commission governs competition between charter planes leaving Canada for destinations abroad. It does not allow a company to charge less than the lowest price charged by Canadian companies. I think it is easy for the Canadian public to understand that it costs less to charter a plane in England, since labour itself costs less than here, and this makes it possible to offer cheaper tickets.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the days since the presentation of the budget of my colleague, the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), a number of comments have been made in various parts of this House concerning the correlation between the various budgeting measures that were presented and the emphasis which this government has placed over the past four years on programs to decrease regional economic disparity. Therefore, with the indulgence of the House, I should like to spend a few moments this afternoon indicating how, in my view, the budget is a significant contributor to the improvement of these

regional economic disparities, and how these programs when taken in concert with the items totalling something over $500 million listed in the estimates will continue throughout the coming year the thrust that was undertaken in 1969 in order to attempt at least to provide a greater measure of equity across this country and to level out some of the disparities which have plagued this country literally from its very beginning.
In connection with budget measures specifically, it is a fact, of course, whatever arguments may be put forward, some legitimate and some perhaps not quite so legitimate, that the Minister of Finance was on solid ground when he forecast there would be differences of opinion regarding the effectiveness of the various measures he introduced. Other speakers in all parts of the House will, I am sure, be commenting on these particular issues, but I should like to point out to the House that there are certain elements within the budget that, in fact, can be forecast with precision and accuracy. The first of these is that, given the concurrence of this House, and I have not the slightest doubt that this will be granted, as of the beginning of April our old age citizens will have a basic pension increase to $100 a month each and considerably more than that if in fact they are entitled to part or all of the guaranteed income supplement.
The second point is, of course, that there will be a very large number of Canadians, particularly in the lower earnings bracket, who will gain substantial tax relief from these measures. Here again, it is possible to make this kind of forecast with complete accuracy. The third point is that there will be considerable improvement, and I hope it will be considerable, in respect of the measures taken to reduce the high cost of living.
I mention these three because they have a direct relationship not only to my responsibilities as the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, but also because I come from the province of Newfoundland where I am well aware of the value of these measures and of how welcome they will be. This, it seems to me, is as much a part of fighting regional economic disparity as are the industrial incentives and economic measures so frequently talked about and referred to-indeed, I regret to say, almost to the exclusion of any thorough examination of other aspects of the regional economic expansion program.
Those of you who come from the Atlantic provinces, and I am sure I would not find any disagreement from either my colleagues from Newfoundland or, indeed, from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) on this score, will know that we have within the Atlantic provinces, apart altogether from the present problems which are very acute and very severe in terms of unemployment, what I call a significant residue which is a reflection of past industrial inequity. In other words, we have a great many middle-aged to elderly people who are dependent upon these kinds of measures and improvements to them literally for every mouthful that goes into their mouths and, in fact, for the roofs over their heads. Therefore, these significant improvements will, I know, be of more benefit in many respects to people in the areas for which I have a responsibility than in some other areas of the country, even though I am not, of course, discounting the benefits there either.
February 22, 1973

The second point where it seems there is an improvement, far beyond those improvements resulting from the budget of the Minister of Finance, is in that area where we have succeeded in turning over additional moneys to the provinces through the equalization formula. I have heard it said in this House that these amounts are perhaps not large enough. I suppose if one were talking about this in purely philosophic or abstract terms he would certainly have to agree that, indeed, seven of the 10 provinces will need even more in the way of assistance than the Minister of Finance is providing at the present time. Let me remind the House that over the past few years the degree of grants under the equalization formula has increased sharply from what it was even four or five years ago. Under this heading alone, leaving out the amount that will be provided through this particular budget, equalization in the case of Newfoundland today, and I use it because I am more familiar with the figures for that province, amounted to something in the neighbourhood of $130 million or $140 million, and now will probably be over the $150 million mark.
I mention these figures, in a sense, off the top of my head because there is no time for a detailed description. The figures are certainly in this area. Another interesting point when one asks what the federal government and federal agencies are doing in respect of regional economic expansion is that they are helping certain taxpayers across the country. Perhaps again I might refer to the province of Newfoundland and mention the fact that according to the statistics which are available for the year 1972-73, 52 cents of every dollar expended by the government of Newfoundland directly came in one way or another from federal spending. At the moment I am not arguing whether this is an adequate, inadequate or excessive amount. I might be prepared to argue with my colleague the minister in private that it might be greater, but I think it is significant to point out that it is still a very large expenditure in respect of any province of this country in the kind of program which the Minister of Finance has moved ahead on this particular occasion.
As Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, I recognize that one of the things which in fact has been most easy to identify is the plight of the municipalities in many areas where disparities are greatest at the present time. The municipalities have to assume a larger and larger portion of the burden of increased services and increased demands, so therefore any relief which is to be provided by the federal government to the provinces will we hope- and I am sure this will be the case-reflect on the position of the municipalities. In addition, however, there is also the fact that in several regions of this country, particularly those which by agreement with the various provinces have been designated as special areas, the federal government through the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has been making a significant input into the plant of the municipalities in these special areas. It might be surprising to hon. members to hear that in fact the emphasis-and it is understandable why this is so-has been on the industrial incentives.
The fact is that if one takes the infrastructure support provided directly by DREE in one form or another to the
The Budget-Mr. Jamieson
provinces, and couples it with the very important other matters designed to put in place a better social structure for these areas, and takes these two together, in the past year as in the coming year some three-fifths, roughly speaking, of the total budget for regional economic development will in fact be going into assistance to municipalities of various sizes but usually small to medium-sized municipalities where in fact the need and demand is greatest. It will interest hon. members to know that during the four years in which DREE has been in operation-and effectively it has only been three and a half years that the program has had an opportunity to start taking effect- just less than an amount of $1 billion has been provided to the provinces. The majority of this has been in terms of infrastructure support and the like, has been provided by the program I have talked about in the past few minutes.
In other words, we have recognized what has been maintained by a great many people, long before the concept of DREE was created, that is, that there is the necessity, if one is to draw industry to a particular area, to ensure there is the infrastructure support necessary to induce an industry to come into the area and, second, to help through the provision of the basic services necessary to make that industry grow. Therefore, I believe this is one of the more important parts. If one takes, as I say, the budgetary measures and couples them not only with the plans and estimates for the future but the expenditures to date, it can be seen that a very significant contribution has been made in respect of the reduction of regional economic disparities.
Let me go on to say that there are unquestionably major problems in respect of the program of regional economic expansion. We have been trying now for some months, indeed the review preceded my assumption of the particular responsibilities, to determine how we can make this whole program more flexible. Perhaps I will be permitted to go into some of these matters in more detail when I appear before the Committee later in the current month or in the month of March. However, I want to re-emphasize this point, because it has been suggested on one or two occasions in this House that perhaps we have not been recognizing the necessity for infrastructure support. I do not like that word, but I am sure hon. members know I am referring to such things as water and sewage systems, aid to land assembly, the building of schools and various other public facilities.
There is another way in which the budget is very significant in terms of what effect it will have in relieving regional inequalities in this country. I refer to the tax measures which the Minister of Finance mentioned on Monday night. When one looks at the difficulties we face in attempting to induce industry on a fairly significant scale into the so-called disparity parts of Canada, it will be seen that there are a number of problems one encounters which are clearly visible but which are very difficult to eliminate and which, in fact, have been with us in one way or another for years. I am sure the Leader of the Opposition in a completely non-partisan sense will probably recognize what I am speaking of because of the innovative steps taken by his government in Nova Scotia in terms of the Industrial Estates and various other agencies of this kind which have been copied in one way or another in other parts of Canada.

February 22, 1973

The Budget-Mr. Jamieson

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not only in other parts of Canada, but right here in Ottawa.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In the short time I have, Mr. Speaker, let me give you what are in my view some of the problems with which we must cope and which I hope we can resolve. The first is in respect of the degree of entrepreneurial skills, talent and initiative which exists in a particular region of this country. If one looks at the disbursements which have been made under the incentives program it becomes perfectly obvious that one of the difficulties we face in many areas, even where we are not only willing but anxious to make expenditures in terms of attracting industry, is in respect of the very small number, relatively speaking, of applicants who come forward seeking this kind of aid. I think there are very good reasons for this. Some of them have to do with the fact that in the case of some small industry there might not be the capability in terms of talent, staff and the like to do the necessary projections, studies of potential markets and the whole range of things which are necessary before one can put a new industry in place.
Another significant point stands out very clearly when one looks at the incentives which have been provided. By and large, the DREE program has been most successful where it has had some direct application in respect of the upgrading of resource-based industry; in other words, where there has been a reasonably solid base such as in the fishing industry. It has been possible there-and there has not been a significant lack of initiative on the part of entrepreneurs-to put in additional funds to undertake expansion. However, the further one becomes removed from the resource-based industry the more one seems to attract what are sometimes described as footloose industries, that is those which can locate in one place in Canada as well as another, and it becomes apparent that the entrepreneurialship is one of the things which is badly needed in many parts of the country.
The next point-and here I return to my observation of a few moments ago about the assistance in the budget-is to try to determine what degree of assistance is necessary in order to change an entrepreneur's or a company's mind about a proposed location in favour of one where it is desirable to build up an industrial enterprise. This is again a very difficult question. I mentioned a few moments ago that we do have various agencies, somewhat comparable to those established in Nova Scotia but located across the country and also located in the "have" provinces as well as the "have-nots", which are also in the business of offering incentives and inducements of one kind or another in order to keep industry active in their regions and to expand. I would naturally assume that each province, whether or not it be more affluent than some of the others, will still want to get a large industrial base.
So, therefore, one of the things that becomes apparent is that this competitive situation which exists, not only between the larger and the smaller provinces but between the smaller provinces themselves, is in many respects detrimental to the whole attempt at getting some form of regional economic expansion. I believe that it will be and

is possible to pit, as it were, the more affluent provinces against the "have-not" provinces in this regard and to do a good deal of shifting, even within the depressed regions of affluent provinces. But one of the real dangers we have discovered, and it is perhaps one of the failings of our federal-provincial system, is that two or three "have-not" provinces compete amongst themselves, and the only winner in that kind of situation is the entrepreneur or the promoter. So one of the things which is important, and what we are seeking to do, is to try to bring some rationality to the industrial development efforts of the provinces, so that far from imposing our will on them we will nevertheless be able to arrive at some cohesive policy so that the poor regions will not be played off, as it were, against each other in this search for industrial expansion.
A third point which it is important to examine in detail in asking how the incentives program can be improved is to improve what I describe, for want of a better term, as the industrial intelligence that is available either to the industrial provinces or to other regions of this country. For a very long time, and certainly it goes back in my own memory to the earliest days of Newfoundland's entry into the Canadian union, there has been a tendency to play it by ear when it came to industrial development, to look to anyone who came forward with a proposal and to say: if you are willing to come in, certain assistance will be granted to you. But there has not been either a strategy or the degree of thorough examination necessary to determine whether that kind of industry will be able to survive in the particular milieu or area in which it is being located. Therefore, I see a need across the country for a very thorough job, particularly, for instance, within the Atlantic region and the western parts of the country, for this form of industrial intelligence.
I want to emphasize that what I have said is in no sense meant to convey any criticism of what some industrial organizations within the provinces are doing at present. Their efforts are very commendable and they have had indeed a good deal of success in one way or another in terms of attracting industry and in terms of getting additional jobs. But there is the necessity for some form of over-view to eliminate, if nothing else, this intense, one would almost describe it as exaggerated, competition that can sometimes develop between provinces. Therefore, there is in the programs that I am seeking now to develop in a comprehensive way an attempt on our part to discuss with the provinces how we can be more helpful to them in establishing this form of industrial intelligence.
Another difficulty in terms of regional development of industry is the growing tendency typified best of all perhaps by southwestern Ontario, but also by a few other regions of the country, for what I described in a speech in western Canada in December as industrial incest. In other words, the whole industrial development tends to become more and more interdependent throughout the country. Therefore, one has a situation in which, if you have a great deal of industry, there are many strong reasons why another one will attach itself to that particular complex, and the process grows. Of course, I should say in parenthesis that the transportation problem is basic to all of us and that any re-examination of the regional economic expansion policy cannot be undertaken effectively unless it also examines the transportation question.
February 22, 1973

But even more important than transportation, in the sense that I have been outlining it, is this tendency for industries to group together. Therefore, it is my judgment, and we hope to work in this direction, that we would get agreement with the provinces. This is in partial answer to a question asked a few days ago by the Leader of the Opposition. We would get, in co-operation with the provinces, the capacity to seek out those people who have a communality of interest in terms of a variety of related industries, so that instead of simply seeking to put a particular plant in a particular location we would do a thorough analysis in that region of what, to use the vernacular of the trade, now are referred to as spin-offs or value added, or whatever the case might be. In New Brunswick we are experimenting with such an approach with a good deal of success at present.
One of the things that is clearly necessary in the Atlantic provinces, for instance, is a complete metal working complex, not simply one factory making one part of a metal working complex but a total complex. So the Multiplex Corporation was established with that idea in mind. It will be very important in terms of a large section of this country that we have not merely the industrial incentives to which I have referred earlier but as well the maximum number of concessions of one type or another, be they depreciation, lower tax rates, or whatever they happen to be, because when one puts all of these things together, they are really the selling tools that we will have in order to induce industries to enter into these regions. I am satisfied for my own part that if we are to get away from the resource based industries in the regions of the country that are not in the centre-which is perhaps the best way to describe it-if we are going to get into manufacturing and processing, which I believe we have to do whether we are talking about agricultural products or fishery products, then it can only be done on the basis or in some variation of the routine that I have outlined.
It has been said, and I freely admit, that the incentives program needs re-examination and needs to be updated. I do not make any apologies for the past performance because I think that when we are before the committee it will be possible to illustrate that it has performed reasonably well, but I think it can perform better. There are questions which hon. members in all parts of this House will want to ask, and, incidentally, I would like to get from them advice on some of these things. For instance, it has been suggested that incentives should be paid earlier on in terms of the start of a new project. In its wisdom this House decided, when the DREE legislation was established, that the enterprise has to be 80 per cent in place in terms of its capital assets before it is entitled to a single cent from DREE. Furthermore, the enterprise must be in commercial production for a period of 30 days.
The reasons for having put these provisos in place are obvious, of course. They were designed to ensure that moneys would not be given out before the assets were in place or before there was pretty clear evidence that the project was going to go ahead. In other words, we were not speculating with the taxpayers money. There are those who say that perhaps this kind of policy should be changed, that in point of fact what is really needed is bridge financing, that we should be prepared to commit earlier and to put dollars in before the project gets to the
The Budget-Mr. Jamieson
point that I have outlined. I have some reservations on this score, but nevertheless it is something that is open to question. It may be that we can find a better formula that would help the small businessman in particular who may have difficulty in getting the bridge financing, even on the basis of an offer of assistance from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
The second way in which the program has to be improved is by decentralizing the decision-making processes. All of us are aware-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last time I rose in the House to speak I had an awful lot of fun with members opposite and they criticized me for not talking about the policies of my department. I think I am restraining myself admirably today.
On the matter of decentralizing, Mr. Speaker, one of the things I feel is important is that we should not think about decentralization in the conventional sense. In other words, when one normally talks about the decentralization of a department or agency one thinks about putting a headquarters in Halifax or Moncton and saying that we-are now decentralized in terms of the Atlantic provinces, or putting a headquarters in Edmonton or Winnipeg, and saying we are now decentralized in terms of the prairie provinces or western provinces. What I am looking for is a decentralizing mechanism that will not simply re-central-ize in another part of the country, but which will ensure that there will be trained, responsible people with authority to make the decisions, in the field, so that in particular the smaller entrepreneurs will be able to get assistance and to get it more quickly.
But once again I have to remind hon. members that one of the great concerns expressed in this House when DREE was established was that there be a solid and assured guarantee that public moneys were not being expended on projects which were, at the very best, of dubious value. As a result there has been a natural, understandable and defensible tendency to try to be careful, to centralize, and to take too long in many respects in the making of decisions. So, Mr. Speaker, I am now in the process of trying to find, in consultation with the provinces, just what is the best method by which we can resolve this particular problem.
One of the other difficulties which we can go into at committee stage, with regard to levels of expenditure on incentives, is that there is still not a sufficiently long history behind the program for us to be able to forecast with precision just how many dollars in incentives will actually be spent in a particular year. One of the related difficulties in that regard is, of course, that it is also hard, at any given moment, to assess how many jobs have actually been created, because the lead time may be as much as three years after a grant is offered before an enterprise goes into production. We will need some more experience on the basis of the past three years' records, before we are able to give the House and the public the clearer figures to which they are entitled.

February 22, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Gillies
There is something else that has bothered me since becoming the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, and which I am hoping we will be able to correct in some other way. I believe that we ought to have a greater degree of advice from knowledgeable people in the various regions, first of all as to the kinds of enterprises which are most likely to succeed, something I have already alluled to, and second, advice on many of the specific applications for incentive grants that are received. I would propose that we expand the present National Advisory Board on Incentives, which has been of very great value to us, to the point where we have sources on which we can draw in all the regions-businessmen, various other people, labour leaders and the like-so that they too will have the chance to tell us in specific terms whether such and such an enterprise has a chance for success.
Of course one of the difficulties has been that we have to respect the confidentiality of the records of various companies that come to us, but I would hope there can be some way arrived at so that not only the members of this House but these advisory panels and the like can have the opportunity, under some form of confidentiality, to assess just how meaningful has been the contribution we have made, and how effective any new proposals we make are likely to be. I am aware that there are members of this House who dismiss the concept of regional economic expansion out of hand. I am aware that there are those who believe that the natural forces should be put into play, that they should be allowed to take their course, and that this country should in all probability be polarized around ten or twelve centres within the next ten to 20 years.
Indeed, there are those who say that any efforts such as we have undertaken, efforts both of this government and of provincial governments, in an attempt to change the normal demographic trends in this country are really, as we say in the vernacular of the sea, spitting into the wind. I cannot accept that, Mr. Speaker, and I do not believe that the majority of the members of this House accept it. I think there is a great deal more-

speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the minister, but the 30 minutes allotted to him by the order of the House passed earlier this day have now expired.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in this debate on the budget which is before the House fully aware of the fact that this budget has probably been awaited by Canadians with more expectation than any budget brought down in the last 15 to 20 years. I am not cynical enough to think that the reason for their impatience for it was simply because of the political implications of the budget, but rather because they, the Canadian people, have a great deal of concern about the way the Canadian economy has been managed in the past four years, and about the way that it is going to be managed during the course of the years ahead.
This concern is easily understood when we recall that we have had an unemployment rate for three or four years of 61 per cent, when we note that we have inflation at a rate of 5 per cent, and that it seems to be increasing, when we see that we have regional disparities increasing more and more, and despite the expenditure of millions of

dollars that they do not seem to be getting less, and when we see that we still have in this rich nation far too many people living in poverty.
The Canadian people are very concerned about these problems. Moreover, they are very concerned not only about these things that are so apparent and easily measured, but they are also concerned because they have a feeling that somehow or other economic policy making in Ottawa is out of touch with the reality of what is happening in the world. Canadians know and have seen that the world is changing dramatically. They know that no longer are we in a period of Kennedy Rounds when there was a great thrust for free trade. They know that we have entered a period in which we may well be moving to more protectionism, and when we do not know what is going to happen as a result of the development of the Common Market.
Canadians are aware that their own country has changed dramatically. They realize that more and more people are living in cities, and that more and more employment has to be found in manufacturing, and in service trades to provide employment for the people in urban areas. They recognize that over the last few years a nationalistic spirit has been developing in this country that wonders why such a high proportion of our resources is controlled by people who are not Canadians and who do not live within the confines of this nation. As a result of all these things throughout the country there is a feeling of concern about what our economic policies are going to be.
People hoped to find out in the budget brought down last Monday night that the government of Canada had entered a new period, a period of new ideas, that the government was really taking our problems seriously, and was willing to bring down measures that would solve them. Did they find that in this budget, Mr. Speaker? The answer is clearly no. This is a budget that could have been written in 1952, that could have been written in 1962, and indeed could have been written in any year since the publication of Lord Keynes work, "The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money". This is a budget that holds together without a particular thrust, that does not represent or seem to understand the urgency with which Canadians want an attack made on the economic problems they face in the world today.
What is the purpose of this budget? At the start of his budget speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) said that the budget was designed to lower unemployment, slow down inflation, create faster economic growth, and increase the real standard of living of Canadians. It is the responsibility of the people of Canada and of this House to decide whether or not the budget can succeed in achieving those particular goals. Canadians will only know a number of months after this budget has been adopted, if unfortunately it is adopted, whether or not these goals can be achieved. We, in this House, do not have the luxury of waiting until that time before deciding whether or not we can support this type of budget. For myself, I see little likelihood that the goals espoused by the Minister of Finance in the budget will be reached.
February 22, 1973

How does the Minister of Finance suggest we solve the present unemployment problem in Canada? The basic assumption of the budget is that we can approach this problem in a global way by increasing the aggregate amount of expenditure in the economy. The minister says he is depending on an increase in export trade, on an increase in capital investment, and on inventory buildup as the basis of the thrust for creating the 300,000 jobs which this budget will attempt to create. He said there will be some increase in consumer demand, but he was not looking to it for the basic thrust of the budget in 1973. Mr. Speaker, can we have confidence in the predictions of the Minister of Finance when he says that 300,000 new jobs will be created? It seems to me to be very difficult to have confidence in that projection. We have no budget papers and nothing has been said in the budget about the way in which forecasts have been made. We are not told what proportion of new jobs will come through increases in manufacturing, what proportion will come through increases in export trade and what proportion will come through increases in investment. We must take on faith the projections of the Department of Finance and I, for one, find it hard to do so, given the fact so many projections have been wrong.
In addition given the fact that the Minister of Finance said only last fall that a cut in personal income tax and an increase in expenditure would bankrupt the nation, and that the Stanfield proposal for the constant dollar was an absolutely unworkable scheme, yet accepted these propositions in the budget further shakes my confidence. In view of this performance by the Minister of Finance, one can have little confidence in his statements.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Even if there were not such a dismal record in the field of forecasting and performance, can one be sanguine about the budget when one looks at its thrusts and philosophy in the attempt to create 300,000 jobs? Can one realistically expect the people of Canada to accept a budget that says that one of the important ways of increasing employment this year is through an expansion of exports? There may be an expansion of exports from Canada during 1973, but it is far from certain in view of the recent breakdown in the international monetary exchanges and the devaluation of the American dollar on February 12. We know that there may be an increase in protectionism in the United States and in other countries with which we do business. We know that, in our own monetary policies, there are problems connected with our floating exchange rate, and I wonder if we can keep our dollar floating without creating serious inflation. We know that in Canada we have never had really high levels of prosperity since the dollar floated up in value. Under these conditions are we responsible in placing confidence in any budget that says that one of the major thrusts for increasing employment in 1973 will be through an expansion of international trade?
What are the other reasons for expansion? We do not know how large the increase in capital investment will be in 1973 but, according to indications at this time, it will not be extremely large. There is still a degree of uncertainty
The Budget-Mr. Gillies
among businessmen, an uncertainty resulting from the provisions of the tax reform bill, from the suggested Competition Act and from changes in labour relation laws. People in the business community still are not sure where the government is going. Consequently, we cannot positively count on substantially increased business investment to move the economy ahead. Certainly, we have been looking for an inventory buildup for the last two years, and that inventory buildup has yet to occur. But even if it does, it is an enormously cyclical factor. So, if we are to depend on increased international trade, on increased inventory buildup and increased capital expenditure to get this economy moving again after it had been in dead centre for three or four years, it seems to me we are expecting more than we have any right to hope for.
What do the budget figures actually tell us? They say that the government hopes, basically, to stimulate an expansion in consumer expenditure and, to do that, the minister has introduced a cut in personal income taxes, a cut which, I presume, the government introduced with reluctance, because, as recently as last May, the government thought that cutting personal taxes was not a good thing to do. However, even if one counts the cuts in personal income taxes introduced in this budget, the amount of money that will be taken out of the hands of consumers by the personal income tax system in 1973 will be higher, it is estimated, than the amount taken out in 1972 despite the cuts which have taken place.
In addition, the budget expects to introduce more purchasing power into the economy by cutting sales taxes and excise taxes by about $200 million, out of a total of $3.5 billion. So, that is a very modest cut indeed. The net effect of all these cuts in taxes will be that the total revenues of the government will be $1.7 billion higher than they were last year. Of course, expenditures have been increased throughout the same period; expenditures have a way of increasing faster than revenues. Consequently, this year the budget proposes a budgetary deficit.
The really fundamental question one has to ask in considering this budget and its effect on employment in the economy is: is the deficit large enough to really move this country ahead, to produce the sort of employment that Canadians have every reason to expect and to hope for within the economy. I would argue, that it is not. In the first place, the change in the cash base, as the minister likes to point out, between this year and last year is essentially nothing. Last year the cash needs of the government were forecast at $2 billion, and the cash needs for the government in the forthcoming year will still be $2 billion. We were to see 300,000 new jobs last year and we did not get them. Why would one think that there will be
300,000	new jobs this year, without any change?
On a national accounts basis, the deficit is less than it was last year. Yes, the deficit is actually less than it was last year. On a budgetary basis it will be only $975 million. I suggest to you that a deficit of this size has little likelihood of moving the country forward in the way in which it ought to go. Let us see what would happen in this country on the basis of our present tax system if there were high employment. Where would we be? If the country were operating on a basis of high employment, under the expenditure and revenue pattern suggested by the

February 22, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Gillies
Minister of Finance in his budget we would have a surplus in tax revenue in this country of approximately $1 billion. Even if we were operating today with an unemployment rate of 5.5 per cent, we would probably still be in a balanced budget condition. Considering the revenue and expenditure pattern that the government has brought forward, how can one ever argue that the economy will move ahead?
As I said many times, I do not like international comparisons, particularly those involving the United States. When United States authorities wanted to bring their unemployment rate down they operated with a deficit of 10 per cent on a national accounts basis and brought the unemployment rate down from over 6 per cent to about 5 per cent in 17 months. On a national accounts basis, the deficit which the American government is running with a 5 per cent unemployment rate is twice as high, proportionately, as the deficit projected by the minister for the forthcoming year. In view of this pattern, there is no reason to expect that a deficit of the size projected in this budget will do anything to move this country ahead in a major way.
How long must Canadians wait before a government takes the sort of action that will put the people of this country back to work? We do not need to have a 6.5 per cent unemployment rate in this country three or four years in a row. We do not need to have young people without jobs. What we need is the will and determination to make the economy work. Only a lack of spirit on the part of government has enabled the situation to continue. In Germany there is virtually no unemployment. In Japan there is full employment. In the United States the unemployment rate is down to 5 per cent. Why cannot we do something about the problem in this country?
I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that if a Progressive Conservative government had been in power and had been given the responsibility of bringing down a budget, it would have brought down one that would get this country going again. That budget would have been substantially more expansionary than the budget the government is introducing at this time. Within one year and a half our unemployment rate would be down towards 5 per cent, revenues would be up and we would not be operating so far below potential. Just think what you could do with the extra revenue that full employment would generate. If you had an extra $1 billion in tax revenue, you could start to move old age security payments down from age 65. If you had an extra $5 billion or $6 billion in output, which would happen and which is the real value to the country from a full employment operation, just think what you could do with regard to housing, regionally depressed areas and so forth. It is inexcusable that, after three years, the government is not willing to go on a much more expansionary basis than they have at the present time. If the Conservatives had brought down the budget, we would have removed the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials-

The Minister of Finance says that with his budget he may overshoot; it is a budget that may be too strong. I do not know how it can be too strong. There is no way that there is sufficient stimulation in that budget to bring unemployment down to a level of 4.5 per cent, the figure for which we should be aiming. Even his own estimate is that the unemployment rate would be down to 5.5 per cent. I suppose what the minister is saying is that the budget may be too much stimulation in its inflationary impact.
There is no question that inflation is a very important problem in this nation. However, anyone who thinks that inflation in the nation today is coming from excess demand in the economy certainly is misinterpreting the inflationary situation in totality. That is unexcusable. It may well be a sort of interpretation that will rank with the earlier choice of the present government trying to stop inflation in this nation by creating unemployment. The inflation we have in this nation today, and a very serious problem it is, will be with us unless we take serious action to prevent it.
February 22, 1973

It is an inflation that is caused primarily by cost push, and an inflation that is created by cost push can only be solved by an action that is dedicated and directed toward attacking the particular problems that are causing it. If this party were the government, it would have introduced on budget night a program which would have called for a freeze on wages, prices, dividends and income. We would have an income policy for 90 days so that we could develop in this country a stabilization program that would really get to the heart of the inflation problem of this nation.

We would have used the time of the freeze to consult with the provinces, labour leaders, business leaders and consumer groups to work out an economic stabilization program that would achieve controlling the price rises in this nation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to speak at the beginning of the budget debate.
I would like to take this opportunity to discuss two subjects which are important both for the constituency I have the honour to represent and for Canada as a whole.

February 22, 1973
The Budget-Mr. I. Pelletier

Before dealing with these two important questions, may I say it is a very happy coincidence that I should be one of the first backbenchers on the government side to speak on the budget. I was offered this opportunity, probably, because the first minister of finance of this country was the Hon. Sir Alexander Galt, the member for Sherbrooke in Sir John A. Macdonald's first cabinet.
The county which I represent has been represented by many other distinguished members who have served Sherbrooke and Canada with high distinction. I might mention, for example, the Hon. William Ives, Charles Howard and Maurice Gingues in this connection.

Sherbrooke, often rightly called the Queen city of the Eastern Townships, is the fourth most important city in the province of Quebec. I am very happy, Mr. Speaker, to be able to draw the attention of the government and this House on the economic situation in Sherbrooke and the Eastern Townships during the debate on the budget, a budget which will allow the government to materialize its intentions.
Mr. Speaker, the two questions I chose to deal with are part of the two major objectives stated in the Speech from the Throne and that the government intends to pursue in the coming years in both the social and economic fields.
I will deal first of all with the economic situation in Sherbrooke and the Eastern Townships and, after that, with amateur sport in Canada.
In order to reach tne economic objectives stated, the government of Canada has launched a two-part program. As indicated in the Speech from the Throne, the first part consists of measures to provide more jobs immediately by strengthening and broadening existing programs. As an example, one can quote a substantial seasonal capital works project to be undertaken in co-operation with municipalities and provinces.
In the second part, the government intends to take measures that will add to the fundamental strenght of the economy and can be expected to have effect with a minimum of delay and, again, one can quote as an example the Speech from the Throne where it is said that the government intends to bring in renewed measures to reduce deeply-entrenched regional economic disparities and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion will be decentralized to allow a better identification of opportunities for regional development.
Among the measures which we could single out in that second part, there is one which seems to me to be important and that is the one dealing with already existing programs to encourage research and development in order to increase their efficiency by encouraging innovation in the private sector of the economy, a two-fold important step in a riding which has two universities-one English-speaking and one French-speaking-two community colleges, one French and the other one English, and several other educational institutions.
As to economic growth, and industrial progress in particular, we are well aware of the fact that the Canadian government in agreement with provinces makes a great contribution to the economic growth, because it has many controls which enables it to encourage investment.
[Mr. Pelletier (Sherbrooke).l
If we consider a map of the province of Quebec, Mr. Speaker, we see that the Eastern Townships region is perhaps one of the only regions in Quebec which has not benefited, during the past few years, from significant government assistance. It now ranks among the slower growth regions in this country.
It has to be emphasized that the federal government, under the designated area assistance program, invested several millions of dollars in this region. As regards industrial structures, however, we must admit that the main reason why we are lagging behind in terms of economy is that the amounts granted were far from being sufficient to create a substantial impact.
Considering data related to employment in the manufacturing sector, we see that Sherbrooke is in a position much worse than many other regions throughout Canada and increased government assistance would be very useful and have pretty good results.
Between 1965 and 1972, employment in the manufacturing sector in Quebec has risen by 7.4 per cent while it dropped by 10.8 per cent in Sherbrooke. Therefore, if the manufacturing sector is important, our region is becoming a marginal area and we can prove, in the light of available information, that the city of Sherbrooke can in no way expect to have an economic recovery without substantial grants from the federal government.
For several years, the Eastern Townships have been studied from a social, economic, cultural, industrial point of view.
In the recently published white paper on socio-economic conditions in the Eastern Townships, we find the main reasons why the Eastern Townships are behind on an economic level, in comparison with other areas of the country. It must be pointed out that the industrial structures are one of the reasons for that economic slump.
We all know that the textile industry as well as the pulp and paper industry have always been and are still among the most important of the district. Now, we know that though both industries have experienced a certain stability in recent years, it must be admitted thanks to the intervention of the federal government, they have not increased the number of jobs and it is easy to understand why there is at the present time a surplus of manpower in that area.
We see anomalies such as, for instance, where the average annual salary paid in the clothing industry of the area is $2,122 lower than the national average, which is $5,492.
This, I respectfully suggest, shows to what extent these traditional industries have paid such low wages in our area.
It is true that the Sherbrooke area has developed an important tertiary sector, but unfortunately the secondary sector has progressed so slowly in recent years that there has been practically no economic progress.
It is obvious that in order to restart the economy, there will have to be some quick and important government action.
The present Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) said not so long ago that the tertiary sector cannot develop if the secondary sector is not in good shape.
February 22, 1973

Regional expansion programs should be timed in keeping with the national economic situation. The federal government has, on one hand, situation programs for the purpose of coping with cyclic variations and on the other hand, national expansion programs to change economic structures of a region at a given time and at long term.
As a result of delayed application of structural programs in many cases (regional development), the government now lacks significant possibilities for making public investments more profitable; businessmen are well aware that there is a strategic timing for investments, which is often determined by the situation.
I therefore believe that we should take these two important factors into consideration for our investments in industrial infrastructures, on the one hand the economic situation of the country as a whole and on the other the situation proper to a specific region at a specific time.
Nationally, 1973 should be a good year for private investments and consequently a good year to support efforts for economic expansion in the Eastern Townships.
It could be useless to think of investing industrial development funds in Sherbrooke without knowing whether or not there will be private investments, which as I have said, depend on the national overall sitation. Just as it could be useless to invest capital in places that are not prepared for them.
Ideal conditions exist in Sherbrooke at the present time, and there is urgent need for action, as a result of the national situation as well as the sad state of the regional economy and the rational requests expressed by the people of the Eastern Townships in the last few years.
Sherbrooke is the capital of the Eastern Townships; the riding encompasses an area which has seen an almost unique migratory movement in Canada. One can say that the Eastern Townships encompass eight ridings, of which seven are rural and one urban. The seven rural ridings are now losing their population to the urban riding of Sherbrooke. In addition, as a result of the stratification of ages, we must welcome a high percentage of young people who flood the labour market.
In 1972 alone, those two factors put together led to an increase in the number of employees in Sherbrooke from 49,244 in January 1972 to 59,100 in 1973. This increase therefore exceeds 20 per cent. Thus 7,449 jobs were created last year to employ this manpower, but as we can easily notice it was not sufficient and in January 1973 the unemployment rate in Sherbrooke was between 11.6 and 11.8 per cent.
Two firms among the most important in the region are now threatening to close down sometime during the year. The university hospital, otherwise recognized throughout Canada, would dismiss about 200 persons and nothing serious is provided as a replacement.
However, there is hope since three firms that would create about 400 jobs would come to Sherbrooke if they were attributed 45 acres of serviced land in a regional industrial park-which indeed has been seriously considered for several years-whose plans are now available.
The Budget-Mr. I. Pelletier
Other industries have expressed their intention to settle eventually in an industrial park in Sherbrooke. This industrial park was recommended in a $250,000 research report sponsored by the federal government in the riding of Sherbrooke. Without help, the city of Sherbrooke can absolutely not equip the industrial park or even provide 10 per cent of the $5 million needed for this project.
The rationalization works necessary to implement the project have come to an end; we have furthermore received a recommendation from the Quebec Planning and Development Bureau that would like to finance it through the special areas programs.
Mr. Speaker, there are also enormous touristic possibilities in the region that numerous studies made in recent years have always properly stressed. We have there unlimited riches if we know how to exploit them rationally. The intentions of the government, through the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, to stimulate this industry in Canada give new hopes to our region.
The situation which I just described raises, on the social point of view, a number of real difficulties which soon will have to be considered.
The white paper published by the Quebec Planning and Development Bureau stated that 20 to 25 per cent of the Eastern Townships population are now living in poverty. In other words, 50,000 people in this region are living below what is considered to be the subsistence level.
As I said earlier, the current unemployment rate has reached alarming proportions since it amounts to 11.6 or 11.8 per cent of labour, and over 40 per cent of the jobless are under 25.
From the annual report just published by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, it is obvious that great progress has been achieved through the programs implemented by this department in the 23 "special areas" throughout the country.
In the recently published annual report of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, one can read:
There are important signs that progress has been made in the effort to strengthen the economies of the slow-growth regions of Canada. A number of key indicators in these regions have begun to move in an encouraging direction,
And further on, the report reads:
The experience of the past three years has made it clear that any effective regional development policy must contain certain key elements. It is clear, for example, that regional development policies and programs require close and continuing intergovernmental co-operation. Such co-operation is essential if confusion and conflict are to be avoided.
And the conclusion is as follows:
One other important fact is clear. Regional development cannot be simply an effort to make all regions similar in their growth. There are important differences in the aspirations of people who live in various regions of Canada. Any effective regional development policy must not only take these into consideration, but also recognize that the quality of life desired by the people of the region can be-
-different.
The development approach taken in each region must recognize this key fact and build upon it.
These, I submit, are clear and specific examples of the type of intervention to which the federal government has

February 22, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Grafftey
resorted for the past few years and which have been successful. We have enthusiastically welcomed in the Speech from the Throne those proposals which are intended to reduce unemployment, check inflation and strengthen the economy.
Through our adoption of the present budget, we shall be able to carry out in many parts of the country projects on which the people have been consulted but which must also, from an economic point of view, be undertaken in the nearest future. This, I suggest, is the economic situation in the constituency which I have the honour to represent.
A joint intervention by the government of the province of Quebec and the federal government has become urgent. Whatever the government mechanisms used to correct the economy of this area, it is imperative that this be done as soon as possible.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks, I would like to congratulate my neighbour from Sherbrooke. I think his maiden speech in the House was in French and I would like to take this opportunity to offer my sincere congratulations to him. Even though his opponent during the last elections was a great friend of mine, I take this opportunity to wish him the best of success in his political career.
Mr. Speaker, at the present time, as well as during the last election, the most important problems for all Canadians are unemployment, inflation and regional expansion.
Our problems remain the same as they were at the time of the last election and they are the result of bad administration of the Canadian economy, whereas adequate policies which were proposed to everybody by our leader and our party should solve those problems.
I can only repeat most emphatically what has already been said. In my view the present debate is an important one because the questions that were important at the time of the election, notably those of unemployment, inflation and regional disparity, are the very questions of concern to the Canadian people at the present time. The same question that was concerning the Canadian people at the time of the election more than anything else, namely the maladministration of the Canadian economy by the present government, is of equal concern today. That is why the budget debate is of such importance not only to the members of this House but to all Canadians.
I would be the first to admit, along with many of my colleagues on this side of the House, that in the short term there are obviously many attractive items in this budget. They are attractive and desirable politically, economically and otherwise-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Wait for the "but".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, there will be plenty of "buts". Members on this side of the House who have preceded me noted time and time again that there is nothing in this budget to alleviate, in the long run, basic problems of unemployment, the cost of living and regional disparity.
As I listened to the minister responsible for DREE a few minutes ago I could not help but feel his whole speech was nothing more nor less than an indication of why DREE has not worked. I repeat, as most members on this side of the House said before me, there is nothing in this budget in the long term that will alleviate unemployment, the cost of living and regional disparity. One might ask why. It is because the budget, in itself, is not expansionary enough to begin to correct any of these conditions.
There are other questions I should like to ask, Mr. Speaker. Where in this budget are the incentives to Canadians to invest in the Canadian economy? If we are really interested in creating a viable economy in this country, which in turn will create more good jobs and I mean good jobs for Canadians, we must do something about developing secondary industry. Surely, one of the first and basic things we do through a budget is to create an atmosphere which will encourage Canadians to invest in Canadian industry and in the Canadian economy. I ask the minister, as people will ask from coast to coast, not just those in this House, where are these tax incentives? This question will be repeated time and time again because there are no long-term solutions in this budget to the basic, economic questions facing the Canadian people.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is a cosmetic job.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If there are no long-term solutions in the budget it is because, as was said by the speaker who preceded me, there are no long-term forecasting procedures in the Department of Finance. We have seen time and time again over the last few years that the United States has outperformed us in areas of regional disparity, inflation and unemployment. I suggest it is because the United States has exercised, not necessarily with bureaucratic control but with leadership, certain percentage guidelines in these areas of inflation and unemployment. Where is the leadership in respect of guidelines shown by this Minister of Finance and this government? I suggest they do not have any and that we will drift along in the same old unimaginative way. There are no long-term forecasts and no guidelines, and we compare very badly with what we see going on in the United States.
Let me remind this House of one of the things that struck me most forcibly, and this is an important consideration. While I have noted, as have other hon. members, that certain transfers are to be made to the provinces, basically speaking this budget does not realize that very often the action is at the provincial and municipal levels. This budget does not recognize the responsibility of the provinces. It is my contention that because of the lack of realization of provincial responsibility we are really not going to achieve any tax cut, because provinces will be forced, much sooner than later, to up provincial taxes. This government does not recognize the duty and responsibility of our colleagues and confreres at the provincial level. I want to stress the importance to hon. members of the House and the Canadian people of watching how this
February 22, 1973

budget, directly or indirectly, will force provincial Prime Ministers and Premiers to increase taxes. This will result in virtually no tax cut for the Canadian people at the end of the year.
Without getting too specific in this budget debate, although sometimes we can argue from a specific to the general by taking examples, I should like to touch upon three problems in my area which are national problems that faced this country during the last election. Very often politicians at the local or constituency level are accused of being narrow or parochial when they discuss what they think are problems of their constituency, but soon find out after coming to Ottawa that they are problems facing and harassing the constituencies of Members of Parliament from coast to coast.
I want to refer to designated areas, health care services and unemployment insurance. It was some time ago that Mr. C. D. Howe said "what's a million", and during the intervening time the government has wasted millions in faulty handling of an aircraft carrier and other things. I am talking about something much worse than that. In a short 15-minute budget speech I do not have the time or the right to document this waste with the Clerk of the House, but I categorically claim that in these three areas which affect not only my constituency but the whole nation, that is designated areas, health care services and unemployment insurance, because of the gross mismanagement of this incompetent and tired administration we are wasting annually over $4 billion in tax money.
Let me first of all refer to the unemployment insurance issue.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You can sit over there and make fun of these things, but I am talking about some pretty serious matters.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mai de tete.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think I need comment on that sort of remark in this House, Mr. Speaker.
While we can talk about the run on the unemployment insurance fund and the maladministration of this fund, I simply talk about the main issue, as did the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), unemployment. However, there are some other things which must be brought to the attention of this House. There was a day about ten years ago when there were unemployment insurance commission offices well placed throughout this country. But to satisfy the bureaucrats much more than to satisfy the will of the people, many of these offices were shut down in the name of efficiency, decentralization or centralization if you like. The fact is that in many constituencies across Canada such as mine-constituencies containing towns with a population of 15,000 people-there is not one UIC office. However, in the present, as in the past, if one in order to qualify for unemployment insurance must be available for work how in the world, if there are manpower offices in the rural areas and UIC offices only in the large cities, can the fund be policed.
The Budget-Mr. P. Neale
In the province of Quebec and in many provinces of Canada, one has a long and painful wait in respect of unemployment insurance benefits because of the terrible administration by this government and by its inhuman administration. An hon. member laughs, but I suggest to him that the same situation exists in his area. People must wait for weeks and weeks to receive their cheques. Some of them have to go on welfare just because this government cannot administer the fund properly. I am concerned about the day-to-day administration of government services. People in my riding ask, if a government cannot get cheques to people who are out of work through no fault of their own, can it administer and govern in respect of other things in Canada. We might say the same thing about the mail services. It is my view that a $1 billion overrun in the UIC fund is an example of poor administration especially when it involves the shutting down of UIC offices.
It might be more difficult to expose les grandes lignes de ma pensee in a short 15-minute speech before this House this afternoon, let alone the next two items in respect of the $3 billion annual waste in the health and medicare field and in the field of designated areas. What is the background to this sort of thing? We were told in the Mackenzie King era that the members of the NDP were nothing more than Liberals in a hurry.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What era was that?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It could have been in the St. Laurent era or in both eras. We were told in the 1930's in respect of the new deal, and later in respect of the fair deal, that the best way to solve social and economic problems was to have a massive infusion of funds and that things would more or less look after themselves. But that approach does not go far enough. Very often it results in wastage. When you have waste in one program, often needed funds for other programs are denied. Now, what do we have? We have an alliance-I do not care what anybody calls it, whether a coalition or an arrangement, I call it an alliance-between the NDP and the Liberals with an obvious result. What will the result be? In the area of health care services and in the field of designated areas-
