subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that I have been limited to 15 minutes, it is not my intention to take the time of this House with pious platitudes about this budget. Suffice to say that it is with considerable reluctance that I offer my support to it. My reluctance stems from the fact that while there is something in it for everyone, there is simply not enough of anything. In my opinion the minister, by his own admission in his budget speech, could have doubled most of the goodies without running short of funds.
The minister has said a number of times that his budget is aimed at creating jobs in Canada and he is talking about 300,000 new workers in the next year. As I understand it, there are some 260,000 jobs created per year in Canada by the natural demand of the market place, so really what he is talking about is some 40,000 additional

February 22, 1973
The Budget-Mr. P. Neale
jobs being created in the next year over and above the normal level. This is simply not good enough, and if this government is truly interested in knocking unemployment below 5 per cent or 5 i per cent in the near future, it must look at some other avenues.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to spend the rest of my time introducing a few suggestions which, in my opinion, would go a long way towards creating employment in this country. First, I would like to suggest that the government take a serious look at recreating a Canadian merchant navy. The ocean-going dry cargo merchant fleet has now been reduced to the lowest possible point barring complete extinction-one solitary ship, if we still have that ship. This does not include the shipping on the Great Lakes. In the past a Canadian merchant marine handled significant portions of our overseas trade. A report of the Canadian Maritime Commission shows that in 1947, 20.2 per cent of the total dry cargo Canadian trade-excluding trade of the United States-was carried in ships of Canadian registry. By 1953, this percentage had dropped to 4.3 per cent. The latest figures that I have seen show the absolutely ridiculous figure of .2 per cent. Meanwhile, ships of foreign registry have captured significant portions of our trade, including ships of German, Greek and Norwegian registry plus the fantastic number of runaway flag ships.
It is incongruous that the Liberal Minister of Veterans Affairs, the Hon. Ian MacKenzie said at the end of the World War II:
We are not going to repeat past mistakes. It is the determined policy of the present government that Canada is in the shipbuilding business for good. The navy and merchant marine that you made are going to be maintained and expanded. The ships you built will carry Canada's trade to the ends of the world, creating employment and opportunity for Canadian workers.
Here is a statement by a responsible government official that failure to build a merchant marine in the past was a mistake. It is also stated that we are to be in the shipbuilding business for good, and that the merchant marine is to be maintained and expanded. Employment and opportunity for Canadian workers are pledged by the solemn word of one of the highest government officials. What was said 24 years ago is still very true, even more so. The discrepancy between promise and actuality can not longer be tolerated. What is the state of affairs with regard to other shipping using Canadian ports to move Canadian goods? Here, Mr. Speaker, are a few glaring examples.
No one example better illustrates the situation than the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Having grown enormously rich over the years at the expense of our natural resources, this international company is now busily engaged in swelling its corporate treasury to the detriment of the vast majority of the Canadian people. How does this work in the case of ships? In the late 1960's, the CPR set up a dummy tax haven, a 100 per cent controlled subsidiary, called CPR Bermuda Limited. Why did the CPR go to this trouble? The answer is simple. There was a lot of dough in it for them, since in Bermuda the maximum annual corporation tax is a paltry $560. In order to take the maximum advantage of this fact and to demonstrate their dollar patriotism, CPR Bermuda Limited constructed in the past five years a merchant fleet of

871.000	dead weight tonnage and has on order an additional 360,000 dead weight tonnage.
Here are the details of this "CPR Bermuda Merchant Marine": Lord Mt. Stephen, a 71,000 dead weight tonnage tanker, on charter to Shell Oil and British Petroleum; Lord Strathcona, a 71,000 dead weight tonnage tanker, on charter to Shell Oil and British Petroleum; R.B. Angus, a 13,122 dead weight tonnage bulk carrier, to take lead concentrates and lumber to Japan; Pacific Logger, a
16.000	dead weight tonnage log and lumber carrier, on long term contract for service between the Pacific coast and Japan; T. Akasaka, a 58,000 dead weight tonnage bulk carrier, to carry ores and particularly coal from Australia to Japan; W.C. Van Home, a 58,000 dead weight tonnage bulk carrier, to carry coal to Japan; Port Hawkesbury, a 250,000 dead weight tonnage supertanker, on long term charter to Gulf Oil Limited; and T.G. Shau-ghnessy, a 250,000 dead weight tonnage supertanker. None of these ships were built in Canada. Not one flies the Canadian flag. None employs Canadian sailors. Most carry Canadian raw materials for the benefit of foreign manufacturing industries, and the profits from all this activity are tax free in Canada.
The largest forest products complex in the world, namely MacMillan, Bloedel and Powell River, has followed a similar practice in a smaller way in the province of British Columbia. This company has had three large ships built in Japan using subsidies and write-offs, so that the cost to the company is minimal. The ships have been named after the chief executives of the company, for example, the H.R. MacMillan, named after the past president, the J.V. Clyne, also named after a past president, and the N.R. Crump. I hope I do not have to explain who he is. These ships are all registered in Bermuda and the company pays minimal taxes to that country, some $560 per year according to my information. I am also reliably informed that there are no Canadians hired on any of these ships and that, in fact, all the crews are of foreign extraction, paying their taxes to a foreign country and spending their wages outside of Canada. This, to my mind, is despicable and a disgrace and these companies have the gall to fly Canadian flags from the poles on top of their office buildings.
It seems to me that I recall statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the last election to the effect that he would seriously consider a Canadian merchant marine if there was no need to subsidize it. You know, Mr. Speaker, some people in this country have a funny idea of priorities. It is proper to subsidize, through the DREE program, large multinational companies which do not need the subsidies, but it is not proper for the Canadian government to build a merchant navy owned by the Canadian people if subsidies are necessary. I should like to point out that to my knowledge every country in the world which has a merchant navy subsidizes it, including even landlocked countries such as little Switzerland.
I propose to this government that it build a federal government sponsored and financed Canadian merchant marine, built in new, technologically advanced shipbuilding complexes on both coasts. Such a national investment would mean thousands of jobs for our skilled shipyard
February 22, 1973

workers and thousands more in other industries; the development of modern technology in heavy industry such as steel, the electrical industry, machinery, and the industrial use of computers; control of the disposition of our foreign trade, which is 25 per cent of our gross national product. Canada would then be in a position to become the vital link in an Asian-European land bridge. It would also mean the development of Canadian raw materials, such as coal, iron ore and copper in Canada, and the extension of secondary industry. It would mean the end of the huge drain in our international balance of payments, which totals $313 million in the 1965-67 period, because of our deficit in the ocean shipping account. It would mean permanent tax revenues, business for ship suppliers and merchants, and much less unemployment insurance expense. It would also mean increased personal income and corporation taxes in Canada. Truly, we cannot afford not to have our own merchant marine.
Now, I would like to raise the problems created by the lifting of the ceiling on interest rates in this country and the fantastic interest rates that finance companies are allowed to charge, a rate of 2 per cent per month on the unpaid balance. In round figures, the Canadian people owe $15 billion in consumer debt-this does not include mortgages on houses-upon which they are paying an average rate of 16 per cent, mostly to foreign owned finance companies which pay very low income taxes to the federal coffers. This means that the working people and the poor are losing $1 billion per year from their purchasing power, most of which is leaving this country in profits and dividends.
I specifically mention the working people and the poor because, in the main, they are the ones who have to buy on credit. The businessman, most of the time, has the cash to purchase consumer goods. He also has a wholesale card in his pocket and saves from 30 per cent to 50 per cent when buying from the wholesaler, and usually saves the sales tax. So once again, the workers and the poor are being ripped-off with the tacit acquiescence of this government. I would strongly urge that the government seriously consider rolling back interest rates to those charged by credit unions in this country.
There is another way that employment can be created and pollution controlled at the same time. I would like to give one small example. Those hon. members from the west coast know that there is a great fear that the Fraser River is on the way to total pollution, created, in the main, from the dumping of raw or primary treated sewage by the many cities and communities lining its banks. Some eight or nine years ago I wrote to the department of the interior of the United States for a report on the pollution and clean-up of the Willamette River in the state of Oregon. I learned that the river is less than one quarter the size of the Fraser and it cost some $400 million to reclaim it. You can imagine how much it will cost the taxpayers if we are stupid enough to allow it and the Strait of Georgia to become polluted. The cost will run to billions of dollars.
The latest figures I have seen on the cost of building secondary treatment plants on the Fraser River is $88 million, and sadly everyone says that that money cannot be raised. I suggest to the government that some of the 25789-27
The Budget-Mr. P. Neale
corporate rip-off funds be given to the municipalities as grants to assist them in saving that river and its valuable salmon runs, instead of waiting until it is polluted and then having to spend billions to reclaim it. This situation is probably true in other areas of this country.
I would like now to talk briefly about pension plans and how they could be used to create employment. There are, I understand, some $11 billion in funded pension plans in Canada and some $4 billion in non-funded plans. Most of these plans are beyond the control of the workers who are putting their money into them. These plans are either controlled by insurance companies or by the employers who arbitrarily set them up. I know that lately some unions have been able to negotiate trustee set-ups to administer their pension plans, but these plans only cover a small percentage of unionized workers. We all know that only one third of the Canadian work force belongs to unions in this country, so very few of them have this kind of protection.
The worst offenders in this respect are the CPR and the CNR. These two companies have absolute control of their employees' pension plans and callously and intentionally invest the moneys in low return areas. My understanding is that the return on investment for both these plans runs from 21 per cent to 3 i per cent a year. The companies are very happy with this set up because they do not put up their share of an employee's contribution until he reaches retirement age. They have been able to use this money for their own interests during all the employees working years and only have to pay retroactively an amount equal to their share, plus what that amount would have earned during the work life of the employee. You can readily see that it is to the advantage of these two companies to keep the return on investment as low as they possibly can.
The CNR is a publicly owned corporation, and it is a shame on succeeding governments of this country that this situation is allowed to persist. This government can set an example by ordering the CNR to allow the employees, through a trustee set-up, to have some say in the investment policy to be followed in respect of their money. Just think of the result, Mr. Speaker, if these pension funds were made available at only 6 per cent so that workers could borrow the money to purchase or build houses. Think of what this could accomplish. First, there would be an upsurge in housing construction in Canada, creating thousands upon thousands of jobs, not just in the construction of these houses but in the manufacture of all the component parts of the house. Second, it would double the return to the pension fund, thereby making it possible to pay higher pensions, which, in itself, would increase the purchasing power of the retired workers and would also allow for a reduction in their retirement age covered by the plan. This in turn would create more vacancies which could be filled by the young people who are presently drifting around this country disillusioned and frustrated, trying to find work.
The same principle could and should be applied to all pension plans in the country so that the contributors to the plans could receive some of the benefits accruing from the investment of their moneys instead of the monster corporations and foreign-owned insurance companies reaping them all.

February 22, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Railton
There are many other issues that I could raise, including improved facilities for bulk loading in the port of Vancouver to stop the drain of shipping and handling of goods now flowing to the ports of Seattle and Portland. But, Mr. Speaker, I have taken enough of the time of the House on this occasion. I just hope that the government will seriously consider some of the recommendations that I, and other members of the New Democratic Party, have made to bring unemployment down to an acceptable level. I want to assure the Minister of Finance that an acceptable level is not 5.5 per cent, not even 5.2 per cent, but a much lower figure than that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is my official maiden speech, although I did give a short opinion on the subject of capital punishment some weeks ago. I would still like to congratulate you and your colleagues on your impartiality, and on the distinction which you all bring to the sittings of this House.
Today, we heard the new member of the official opposition who represents Don Valley (Mr. Gillies). I notice that he did not express his opinions in this House until the budget speech had been read. I think hon. members should make a note of that. The leadoff speeches for the Progressive Conservatives, the NDP and the Socreds have also been given. Regarding the first, we heard only criticism, this in spite of the fact that they claimed that our Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) had stolen their ideas. It is obvious that that is not the case. They did not come even half way to meet our proposition, and they had no real method proposed for working out their scheme.
The NDP leadoff speaker supported us very well, but of course he claimed that we had stolen many NDP ideas. This may be so, but that seems to be the function of a party that is doomed to remain in the minority and which admittedly has left wing ideas. So far as the Socreds were concerned, we were blasted all the way. Their main cry was for the introduction of their peculiar economic philosophy, which would require the printing of funny money to put it into practice. So, although we must always impute the highest of moral qualities to other parties, we can see that the attacks of the Official Opposition are simply an attempt to confuse the electorate, and hopefully to bring down the government, in this way getting their chance to force an election. This is very obvious. They seem so desperate that it is becoming crystal clear that their chance of forming a government is getting slimmer by the hour.
The members of the NDP must be given credit for idealism. They are, in addition, a well disciplined party with an eye to the future. They have temporarily submerged their socialistic anchor, but to be credible they have taken to the marriage bed with a gun, threatening that this may be their last try to make a marriage of convenience work.
To me, the budget is the best one produced by any government, whether majority or minority. The reduction of tax is really 12 per cent. It is definitely a poor man's budget. It is unprecedented in Canada's experience to give a $5,000 a year man a 47 per cent reduction in his income tax, and an $8,000 a year man a 15 per cent

reduction in his tax. The sales tax is family oriented. The lightening of duties on fruits and vegetables is a big blow to high food prices. It is also, as the Minister of Finance stated, a friendly gesture toward our largest trading partner, and now it gives us some reserve for negotiations on all tariffs, and still will not hurt our producers.
My constituency of Welland is right near the Niagara frontier. It is agricultural in some portions, but very well industrialized also. It contains heavy and light industry, with large firms, Canadian owned, such as STELCO and Atlas, and also foreign owned firms such as INCO and Union Carbide.
We also have many medium and small industrial projects in the area. Recently I asked these firms about their reaction to Canada's tax program and to the government's budgetary direction. They have been unanimously in favour of our government's policy to date. They also show statistically that the tax reduction was one of the big factors in keeping unemployment in the area down to a 4 per cent or 5 per cent figure. We have American subsidiaries in our Welland-Niagara area. They employ a great many people. We should realize that we could easily lose all these plants if we use tax discrimination against them. Neither the Welland constituency as a whole not the labour unions in the area want any change in our tax policy. I spoke to several of the unions as recently as Monday last, and I say this House would do well to realize that organized labour in the Niagara peninsula is strong and has had excellent treatment. In addition, it is very co-operative with management and government.
I would like to make a plea for closer ties vis-a-vis Canada and the United States, if only on a friendly basis. In the Welland area many Americans own summer cottages. We have grown to like each other. Every slap in the face in our press hurts them. It must be evident to all hon. members that Americans came to our aid in two world wars. They have policed the world when it was in imminent danger of atomic warfare. Surely, any rebuke or rebuff from us, either verbally or financially, must be a very gentle one.
When speaking of our border with the United States along the Niagara River, I would like to emphasize that we have had in actual fact 100 years of peace. The war of 1812 and the Fenian raids are past. Incidentally, I would like to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I still have my grandfather's homemade powder horn which he made before getting on the train to go down to fight the Fenians. He got there too late to fire a shot. Now, Mr. Speaker, Americans and Canadians pass each other in both directions over great international bridges at Queenston and Fort Erie. Visitors from the United States are happy to enjoy our beaches and northern lakes, while we press south to the great cities of New York, Cleveland, Detroit and Chicago, or head for the southern states and Mexico. What a wonderful continent we have, and what a marvellous heritage we have in Canada.
Just recently a dinner was held in this House supporting multiculturalism. I was unable to be present but I would like to draw the attention of hon. members to the terrific melting pot we have in the Welland riding. In the city of Welland we have 5,000 or more French Canadians. They take very prominent places in the life of the city and in
February 22, 1973

our municipal councils. This is only one race. We have close to 10,000 other people of various origins, Italians, Hungarians, Poles, Latvians, Croats, Estonians, Ukrainians, and representatives of all other middle European countries. They have mixed well with the old German, Dutch and British stock. We have an extremely interesting panorama of languages and cultures. I think it would do any member of the House a great deal of good to visit this area and see how well the principles of bilingualism and multiculturalism work in my constituency.
The area is remarkably prosperous. We have an agricultural economy of no mean proportions, with mixed farming of all kinds. We also have a great deal of vegetable farming, and we have the tender fruit areas. We are trying to retain the grand old orchards and vineyards in the area between the escarpment and Lake Ontario, and the Tender Fruit Association, known to all hon. members, is doing its best to bring the plight of the fruit and vegetable farmer to the attention of the government. We have a wine industry which is second to none in Canada, and which is becoming recognized throughout the world.
Because of our proximity to Lake Erie, a great many people were very worried about the high lake levels and the lack of provision for either public works, subsidies, or insurance to protect against the recent storm catastrophe. However, I have been able to assure these people that we are trying to do something to solve these difficulties.
One of the great public works in my area is the Welland ship canal. This is the fourth one that has been built during the last 200 years. The most recent addition is the bypass which straightens the canal and takes it out of the city of Welland. It now runs straight from Port Colborne to Port Robinson and allows much faster shipping movement. Formerly there were many traffic delays. There were irate citizens in both Welland and Port Colborne waiting for bridges which, in previous years, had to be raised and lowered every few minutes in an attempt to let the ships pass through the canal.
The Welland Canal is part of the great international seaway that takes shipping right up to Thunder Bay and Chicago. It is one of our greatest routes for the shipment of our wheat and ores. It is a tremendous freighting facility not only for internal trade but also for ships coming from every corner of the world. This seaway runs 2,000 miles into the heart of North America.
Building the bypass to avoid the city of Welland has brought troubles in its wake. Though it has provided two tunnels, at great expense, for our automobiles and our rail traffic and supplied a very fine new dock, and though it is going to open on time-thanks to all our efforts-next April, it has left the old canal, which is now abandoned, right in the centre of the city of Welland. The old canal does not flow. It is going to be a static ditch because of the causeway which carries heavy freight lines across the old canal after emerging from the tunnel under the new bypass. This means there is a great likelihood that the old canal will become polluted and unsightly.
So it is the job now of myself and the council of the city of Welland to make sure that the government sees clearly the plight in which the new bypass has left us and the city 25789-27*
The Budget-Mr. Railton
of Port Colborne. For this reason I have been making representations to the government and the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority, along with delegations from the local municipalities and the region, to settle this matter. The fate of unused or abandoned canals in Canada has never been particularly pretty. One of the most recent problems in this regard involved the canal at Cornwall, which concerns Mr. Speaker. After ten years of hard work which involved His Honour, the citizens of the area and the government, a solution was found. I think a solution in our case will be more difficult to come by. I have talked about our local situation, Mr. Speaker. I think all of us should look beyond the localities we represent even though we may come from such lovely spots as Welland, in the Niagara peninsula, which is really a continuation of the golden horseshoe running along Lake Ontario from Oakville to Burlington.
When we look at the world situation, we know that we must trade with the U.S.A. Seventy per cent of our exports go there right now. About 12 per cent go to Europe. There is a smaller percentage going to Japan and the undeveloped nations of the world in Africa and Asia. There is so far very little trade going to China and Russia, but let us not forget that it was our own Liberal government and its leader which initiated the rapprochement between the west and these two great countries.
It will be very difficult for us to export manufactured goods to that remarkable economy of Japan. It will be almost as difficult to find suitable goods to export to the European community. However, the people in our area as well as those in the rest of Canada, hope that if we implement all the parts of this budget there will be a great opportunity for us to continue trade with the United States, Europe and Japan and to find new markets in emerging countries as well as in the two great nations which formerly hid behind the iron curtain.
As a new member, Mr. Speaker, I feel privileged to be taking part in this lively and historic parliament. Frequently the action gets a bit rough. However, what good is a man who will not fight for something? We seem to be successful in channelling this basic human instinct into making this minority government work. All members of this House are obviously good Canadians, so I am confident that our national future is in good hands.
Recently, an hon. member opposite drew a good analogy about the short span of human life on this planet. He said that a length of rope stretching from Lake Ontario to the Speaker's chair represented the total span of life on earth. He showed that the very short, final end of the rope was the length of man's time in the evolutionary scale. For a few minutes I was worried that his rope might have a noose on the end which he might tighten around the necks of the government supporters.
This picture can be transferred from the past to the future. At some time not too far into the future our knowledge of astronomy and space technology will pierce the secrets of space, time and even immortality. In my mind there is no place in Canadian society for resigned acceptance of eventual human decadence. So, Mr. Speaker, even the trivia of party politics arid the present budget debate are small but necessary evolutionary steps in the upward progress of mankind.

February 22, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Blenkam

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget speech we listened to the other night will do absolutely nothing to correct what I consider to be one of the most serious problems affecting young, newly married Canadians who want to raise a family. Hon. members on the other side suggest that the budget will deal with unemployment and inflation. They suggest that there are adequate proposals in the budget to handle those problems. For the few minutes allotted to me may I direct the attention of this House to the serious problem of housing, the cost of housing in our large urban centres, in particular in and around metropolitan Toronto.
When I raised this matter in the House the other day, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) suggested that he had said nothing about housing in the budget and that Bills C-133 and C-135 would be helpful. Anyone who has read those bills will realize that they will do absolutely "zip" to solve the problem: they are just tinker bills. One bill creates an unworkable mortgage exchange, no doubt dreamed up by a foggy bureaucrat somewhere, and the other attempts, with a lot of financial salve, to do something about urban development; in other words, something about low-income housing. But it will not do anything that has not already been tried.
It became evident throughout the election campaign that municipal authorities, provincial authorities, people in apartments, people all over the country, including developers, had isolated the problem which has to do with lack of serviced land in and around the cities. The government has proposed nothing since the election, either in the budget or in any bills on the order paper, that will deal with this problem.
Municipalities encompassing growth areas, and the provinces, are clearly short of money. Because they are short of money they cannot build rinks, community centres, sidewalks, sewers, water mains, rapid transit and similar facilities; therefore, they are not able to approve plans of subdivisions presently filed, registered and ready to go. To be sure, under the Central Mortgage and Housing legislation provisions there is an arrangement whereby municipalities will be lent 75 per cent of the cost of constructing sewers. That provision is to help with the construction of sewer mains. But that kind of loan affects the debenture credit of a municipality; as a result, the provisions of the act in this respect are totally useless.
Developers such as the McLaughlin company, the Erin Mills company, the Markborough company and hundreds of others, have subdivision plans which are ready to be put into operation. They are ready to do something about this problem. And what has this government suggested as a solution? Land banking. We have all sorts of land banked around the metropolitan centres of this country, ready to go and ready to be developed-and this government has done nothing about it. It has done nothing about the $16,000 it costs for a half or semi-lot, or about the $18,000 or $20,000 it costs for a single-family house lot. Has this government done anything about the fact that, because we are only bringing onto the market less than one-third of all residential lots required, by next year the price of residential lots in Toronto will rise to about $24,000? No, Mr. Speaker, the government has not done a thing. It has no program. Right now in the metropolitan
[Mr. Railton.l
Toronto area, unless you happen to be privileged or wealthy, with money in the bank, you cannot afford a new house. Only 4 per cent of the citizens of that area can afford to buy a new home.
Something must be done. The government has suggested that $100 million a year should be used for land banking. They should be making grants to municipalities. They should be turning over to municipalities some of the money they have for programs that will service land and get land on the market. When I asked the minister about this during today's question period, he had no answer. He said maybe we will have some land available soon.
Let us talk about his land banking scheme for a moment. The minister will have land available. He is going to build new cities. Maybe in two years he will acquire the land. Maybe after five, six or seven years, when he organizes things, he will service some of that land. I suggest it will be at least ten years, and perhaps longer than that. It may take the 20 years that Malvern took before any of this land in his famous land bank gets on the road so far as development is concerned. This is the record of the government in dealing with this problem.
The social damage caused by this government in its housing program is probably the greatest it has ever caused. During the election campaign, I went into apartment buildings. I want to speak about one of them. This apartment building had on it the sign of the present Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras). It contained 360 suites, fronted two four-lane highways, was faced with red brick, sterile, with a playground which was a fenced-off part of an asphalt parking lot. You would not even put animals in a zoo in those playground facilities. The kids have to ride their bikes in crowded apartment corridors. That is the policy of this government with regard to low-income housing. We have not heard a thing from this government about a backyard for kids to play in, a park or facilities that will make life better for those who are in the less fortunate category of society. We have not heard anything about bringing down the cost of housing.
We should now be talking about the economic cost of housing and not just the social cost. The social costs are serious enough, but we must also talk about the economic costs. The other day I spoke to a man who came into my office and said he needed some help. He could afford to pay a man $130 a week; however, he could not get the man he wanted because he wanted to live in a decent house and drive a decent car, and therefore could not start at that wage level. Even though he would eventually earn $250 a week or more, the man said he could not live in the community with that kind of wage. Here is a man trying to build a business, get ahead and get other people involved in work. The whole problem boils down to inflationary high rents and high mortgages in our metropolitan areas.
I want to say a few words about one of the geatest national disgraces this government continues to allow. I refer to the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials-11 per cent on every brick, every piece of plumbing pipe,
February 22, 1973

every concrete block and every sheet of lathing. We do not now charge tax on food, and apparently this government says we do not even have to pay sales tax on the mix for a cocktail party; but we charge tax on building materials.
The party to my left is going to support a government that believes shelter costs should be taxed. Can they think of anything worse than that? This is a tax on growth areas. It is a regressive tax. It is principally collected from areas of Canada where growth rate and housing problems are most severe. This tax is maximized in areas where costs are already overbearing the price of a house. We need aggressive changes and suggestions. If we are going to tax buidling materials, some of the tax should be rebated to the municipalities or the purchasers of houses so they will at least have a little bit of equity. We did not receive such a proposal, or anything like it, from this government.
The area I come from is sometimes called the golden horseshoe. I suggest to the House that the government has used this area as its golden goose. This area is a source of tremendous tax revenues for this government. Any farmer knows that if you want to get eggs from a goose, you have to feed it. The government's attitude to this growth area, with its tax on building materials, is to take, take, take. It is about time that somewhere along the line the Minister of Finance did a little giving.
The minister must realize that if we are going to attack unemployment, the construction industry can supply more employment than perhaps any other industry. This government's program on employment has been unemployment insurance, LIP, Opportunities for Youth, and so on. However, none of the programs presented by this government have been to build anything that is useful and will get people organized, such as community centres. The other day I received a call from a lady in Malton. She asked if she could get a grant to organize a community centre. I told her that the federal government had pumped $40,000 into her community in the last year, but not a dime for building a facility that would have any permanent value. The programs this government produces do not have any permanent value.
If we are going to build Canada, it is time we looked ahead, took the kind of aggressive action suggested by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) and attacked the social problems of the city, the problems of housing and the cost of housing. I speak on this matter with feeling. I speak on it because I have an element of self-interest in it. As the cost of residential houses keeps rising, and the only alternative of this government seems to be bigger and bigger high rise apartments with more subsidies, I can see the environment in which my own children will grow up. I had a back yard. I had a place to grow, a place to be. Through not having a concrete housing policy and not attacking the problem of making land available, my children will not be able to have a home. That, Mr. Speaker is my concern. That gives me a personal interest. Perhaps I should not be bringing personality into a debate such as this, but I am sure that is the personal interest of every member of this House.
We must get with it. We must demand from this government a concrete proposal for making available land for housing. The problem has been identified. It is time this
The Budget-Mr. C. A. Gauthier
government took aggressive action instead of just relying on old programs that have not worked.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to start by explaining certain points, among them the reasons behind the sub-amendment moved by my. colleague, the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte), who blamed the government for failing to take the steps needed to reduce the national debt and to set up a policy for financing provincial governments that does not lead Canadians at all levels of society and in all regions into constant and progressive debt.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) stated openly in his budget speech on Monday evening that the financial deficit in 1973-74 will be around $975 million, while the non-budgetary needs will amount to $1.25 billion. The overall requirements are estimated at about $2 billion, which is roughly equivalent to those of the current financial year.
At page 18 of the booklet "How your tax dollar is spent 1973-74", there is a table of past, present and future expenditures in connection with the national debt, i.e. what it costs the Canadian taxpayers every year to pay the interest on the national debt.
Here are the figures given in the booklet to which I have referred:
1964-65	(millions of $) $1,051
1965-66	1,111
1966-67	1,191
1967-68	1,301
1968-69	1,480
1969-70	1,717
1970-71	1,823
1971-72	2,010
1972-73	2,175
1973-74	2,581
It is alleged that the national debt is not a bad thing that it is current practice in all countries of the world to get indebted and pay interest to government bond holders because this, they say, keeps the money flowing and above all, these bonds are in the hands of Canadian citizens who profit by them.
Mr. Speaker, until recently the Creditistes were practically the only ones to criticize such a way of thinking and to refuse to consider as normal the indebtedness of the federal government, provinces and municipalities.
In the Labour Gazette of December, 1972, published by the Department of Labour, there is an article written by Mr. Richard Deaton and entitled "Crisis in Taxes".
Incidentally, Mr. Deaton is the director of the Canadian Union of Public Employees and holds a diploma in economics and industrial relations from Wisconsin University. On page 653 of the Labour Gazette, he describes in revealing terms that, from 1950 to 1970, provincial and municipal expenses have been higher than their revenues, whereas the federal government revenues have been higher than its expenses.

February 22, 1973
The Budget-Mr. C. A. Gauthier
In fact, from 1950 to 1970, these revenues totalled about $155 billion against outlays of approximately $125 billion. Provincial coffers took in about $65 billion, but expenditures soared to approximately $80 billion, which represents a total deficit of $15 billion. As for municipalities, their revenues amounted to almost $45 billion, while expenditures were about $65 billion, or a deficit of some $20 billion since 1950.
This is how Mr. Deaton explains the problem and here are the conclusions he draws from the article:
This table shows that at both municipal and provincial levels, total expenditures incurred between 1950 and 1970 exceed total revenues. Only at the federal level is the situation the reverse. Succeeding deficits only increase the debt of administrations and finally result in tax increases. If the "crisis" thus defined only affects municipalities and provinces, it is supported mainly by the federal government which, in part, stands surety for municipal and provincial administrations by consolidating debts and making transfer payments.
The Department of Urban Affairs formally stated: Municipalities have more and more trouble to finance their ever increasing budget. The expenditures of most urban areas exceed their revenue. They borrow or make drastic cuts in public services.
They find themselves in a vicious circle. Each time the property tax goes up, businessmen and "middle class" landlords move to the suburbs, and in order to keep on providing municipal services despite this shift in the tax basis, cities increase even more their taxes ...
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House adjourned, I was reading an excerpt from the publication which deals with deficit spending at various levels of government. The quotation goes on:
Provincial and municipal administrations mainly have blanced their accounts through deficits and by creating debt servicing. From 1950 to 1970, this has only caused the situation to worsen. Thus, the surpluses accumulated during this period, at the three levels of government reached $3.5 billion, while the deficit reached $6.6 billion.
Now with this deficit policy, governments borrow and the debt is growing. From 1950 to 1968, the indirect and direct debt of the federal government went up by 36 per cent; the debt of provincial governments, by 505 per cent, and the debt of municipalities, by 511 per cent. The economists ... keep saying: "The national debt? We owe it only to ourselves". They are missing the point: in fact, the interest on the debt uses up income we badly need for other things.
At present, the cost of servicing the debt alone is the third largest item in public expenditure;
-and when the article was published, we were in second place, but we are now lucky enough to be in third. I continue to quote:
-this money goes mainly to the banks, which are the large buyers of bonds issued by the State in order to cover its deficits.

In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I should like to stress the truth of Mr. Eaton's statements to the effect that the interest that we pay on the public debt goes mainly to the banks, which are the largest buyers of government bonds.
In the budget papers for 1971, table 14, page 56, shows an interesting situation about the distribution of this debt. The table indicates that in 1960, the banks were holding $1,381 million in Treasury bills and that this amount increased to $3,366 million in 1970, namely a $1,985 million increase in favour of the banks.
On the other hand, in 1960, $549 million in Treasury bills were in the hands of the general public, while this amount was down to $218 million in 1970, namely a $331 million drop in Treasury bills held by all Canadians. If you consider the bond market, you find the same tendency.
In 1960, the banks held only $4,421 million in bonds. This amount increased by $3,146 billion in 1970 and reached $7,769 million. On the other hand, in 1970, the general public was holding only $6,484 million in savings bonds, namely a $753 million slump in ten years. It is true that the public which held $3 billion in savings bonds is now holding $7 billion. However, the banks which were holding only $5,802 million of the public debt, are now holding $10,935 million, namely a $5,133 million increase. This means that in ten years, the banks have doubled their assets in savings bonds and are now holding over 40 per cent of the debt. Thus, of the $2 billion in interest that the Canadian taxpayers will pay this year, the banks will cash in over $800 million, which represents about $2,500,000 in daily profits made out of nothing by the Canadian bankers.
The minister himself admits it on page 56 of the budget papers. During the last decade, of the $7,900 billion collected through the issuing of government bonds, the banking system, namely the Bank of Canada and the chartered banks, absorbed all Canada bonds issued as well as a reduction of more than $1 billion of the securities held by other investors.
That is what the minister said. This means that the banking system benefits from the billions paid each year by Canadian taxpayers for the payment of the debt.
Now, Mr. Speaker, how would a Social Credit government finance this public debt? Here is a means available to the government to increase the standard of living of all Canadians without taking anything from anybody, without bringing the economy to a standstill, without bringing about inflation or deflation: it would be to finance public capital by credit advances without interest issued by the Bank of Canada.
One can see immediately that this kind of measure would result in reducing the taxes that the government levies in order to pay the interests on the public debt or its borrowings, and would increase the amounts available to consumers to obtain the goods which would meet their needs.
At this point in the discussion, Mr. Speaker, I would say that although the Creditistes do not get much support for their ideas on the introduction of a national dividend, for
February 22, 1973

instance, they do get some in favour of creating new interest-free credits for financing public capital.
In his book entitled Demain c'est Van 2000 (The Year 2000-Tomorrow), Mr. Gaston Bardet, a professor of applied economics at the University of Brussels, after having studied in depth the banking system, and in the light of the studies conducted in Great Britain by the MacMillan commission and those carried out in Canada in 1939 by the Committee on Banking and Commerce of the House of Commons, came to the following conclusions:
There are therefore two possible methods of financing which are diametrically opposed: one is based on savings, on excess money, the other on anticipating. In the first instance, with regard to private production, control is automatic and depends on the offer of existing capital. In the second instance, it depends on the demand for the most assured primary needs. Thus bank financing is really indicated for the construction of property equipment for the benefit of the entire country. When there is no danger of overproduction, demand really determines the supply. Such are the requirements for housing, roads, bridges, hospitals, schools, forestry, which this time become the regulators of anticipated script money.
It is a matter of consumer loans and no longer one of production. Interest is no longer involved. The country and the community cannot be usurers.
Another economist has considered the problem of government financing and has drawn the conclusions discovered by the Creditistes a long time ago, namely the financing of public capital through new interest free credit.
This principle is stated in The Challenge of Abundance by Mr. Robert Theobald, a book which can be found in the Parliament Library. Mr. Theobald writes as follows:
A government can use three different methods to obtain the funds it requires to meet its obligations. First, it can tax its citizens and institutions, thus gaining possession of their money. Second, it can borrow money from people and institutions and pay interest on the amount it borrows. Third, it can simply create money and use resulting funds to make its purchases ...
The one point on which everybody agreed before 1936 was that the government should never simply create funds. The prohibition against creating funds was based on the assumption that the demand for goods would always be equal to supply as long as government did not interfere with the economy. Keynes destroyed the validity of this assumption when he showed that there was no certainty that the demand for goods would always be equal to the available supply in the rich countries ...
There are other methods that could be used to close any gap between supply and demand. It would be possible to decrease the level of supply without greatly affecting demand by cutting hours of work and leaving wages unchanged. It would be possible to raise the desire for goods by making people feel that more products were necessary for the good life and a decent standard of living. The government could simply take up the slack between actual and potential production by building new schools, by demolishing slum housing and building new accommodation, and by controlling pollution. Because there would be unused resources in the economy, the government would not need to raise this money by taxation or by borrowing, the money could simply be created. The additional funds would not cause inflation, for there is-by definition-no shortage of goods.
This, Mr. Speaker, is the testimony of an American economist, Mr. Robert Theobald, who thinks that it is possible to make money more democratic and to use new interest-free funds for the development and social equipment of the country. If this not the right time to do what
The Budget-Mr. C. A. Gauthier
Mr. Keynes urged so strongly, namely, to "make financially possible what is physically feasible", and I quote:
As a first step, a national financing corporation should be set up in order to provide the funds necessary for the creation of assets for the benefit of society. Thus, jobs would be provided as long resources would last. In a free society, in peacetime, an excess labour force cannot be directed to different occupations, but with education, rehabilitation, a good salary, proper housing, it can certainly be attracted to other occupations, keeping in mind that the GNP can be increased annually.
Never before has our ability to produce, transport, communicate been so great, however, the government's admonitions to tighten our belts inevitably result in restrictions imposed upon producers in various ways. History will show if taxation was too heavy or too complicated. This is why we suggest that for what is called nonprofitable capital goods, a national financing corporation must be set up to meet those needs. This would require very specific terms of reference in order to avoid any conflict with the various financial organizations serving the private sector of the economy which is profit-making-The national financing corporation which would be one of the most important factors in government policies would provide a large part of the money or credits now collected through taxation. Even at the high rates we have at present, taxation is unable to use inactive resources to build a sophisticated road system for example. Moreover it adds an enormous burden to the cost society must pay in interests.
Mr. Speaker, last Friday the hon. Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) said to the House that he would like to be able to finance the building of a Canadian pipeline in the Mackenzie valley but that "he was not a Creditiste and he did not know how to print money".
If the minister does not know how money and credit originate, let him consult his banker who, if he is at all clever and honest, will tell him how the banking system creates credit out of nothing. And if his banker does not know, I will send him a copy of the explanatory brochure published by the Royal Bank of Canada so that he will learn that all that is physically desirable must be made financially possible, and that with a financial system that is true to facts, economic problems would not exist when there is no problem of production.
As the marquis de Serra has written in "Economic chaos and the coming revolution"-

speechtext: He is a bastard!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, but he did write some pretty good sentences. Sometimes, bastards do write something good. It is the dawn of art to express in terms of units called dollars the development of materials, natural resources and technological methods, and it is again the dawn of art to create purely monetary means, among which credit, to facilitate the exchange of various services which will carry out the plans.
Mr. Speaker, if I still have a few minutes, I would like to deal with another very interesting subject. I would have liked to have more time to deal with it thoroughly, but I only wish to touch on it lightly because we read in the budget headlines that its major objective is to reduce unemployment.
In brief, the Minister of Finance is at war with unemployment. He stated that his prime objective was to fight unemployment. But what are his tangible proposals? Nothing very serious, Mr. Speaker, because certainly the

February 22, 1973
The Budget-Mr. C. A. Gauthier
crumbs he gave in his budget will not go very far in solving the problem.
What I think was needed was a reform which would have produced massive shifts toward a more realistic guaranteed income such as, for example, pensions at 60. This would have had a direct effect on unemployment, allowing more than 400,000 unemployed to receive a family salary while at the same time effecting savings for the Treasury. Indeed, if you consider that sometimes it costs both levels of government up to $400 or $500 a month to keep a family going on social welfare-drugs, shelter, clothing and food-when it would cost only a maximum of $325 to pay a pension to a married couple of 60; by thus replacing pensioners between the ages of 60 and 65 by unemployed the government would save while at the same time perhaps reducing the number of unemployed which stands at more than 400,000.
